1:
The title occupies the older voices first. Augustine takes the word rendered presses for a mystery rather than farm equipment, and reads it of the Church: in a press there is pressure, and of the pressure two results, one laid up and one thrown away. John Calvin divides the psalm in two, an exhortation to remember the grace that delivered the people, and then God upbraiding them for refusing the yoke of the law; opinions vary widely, he notes, as to the occasion. Adam Clarke thinks it generally agreed that the psalm was written for or used at the Feast of Trumpets, held on the first of Tisri at the opening of the Jewish year and still used in Jewish worship on that day; he adds the tradition, credited by many learned Christians, that the world was created in that month. Keil and Delitzsch describe the construction instead, combining the lyric quality of one earlier psalm with the didactic quality of another, and account for the abrupt close by the author's habit of ascending to his subject's height and descending into its depth without returning to where he began.

C.H. Spurgeon presses manner and reason both: in tune and measure so that public praise may be in harmony, and aloud, since no dulness should stupify our psalmody nor half-heartedness make it limp — God's acts of love speak more loudly than any words of gratitude can. Matthew Henry adds that we do not come to church to sleep or be idle, our errand being to give God the glory due to his name.

The instruments draw a catalogue from Clarke — the drum, the harp he takes for a sistrum, the psaltery which the Greek rendered a cithara, and the horn, certainly a wind instrument where the two before were stringed. He then turns the verse into an argument: in a representative religion such as the Jewish there was necessarily much outside work, emblematic of better things, but that is no proof it should continue under the Gospel, where the shadows have flown away; a man must be ill off for proofs in favour of instrumental music in church who has recourse to the Jewish ritual. Charles Ellicott corrects the opening phrase to strike up a tune, and notes of the horn that it is the only ancient Hebrew instrument still in use on solemn occasions.

Which day is meant is disputed. John Gill and Clarke read the new moon of the seventh month, the day of trumpets. Ellicott is more cautious: standing alone the phrase might mean the beginning of any month; on the second phrase a long array of authorities gives the time appointed, but in the only other place the word occurs the Latin has after many days, the margin new moon, and two ancient translators full moon — which he thinks better supported.

The last verse of the group is the hardest. Clarke states the difficulty plainly — who heard, and what was heard — and reports that every version but the Chaldee reads the pronoun in the third person, so a modern critic has reformed the text; as to the language, some say Egyptian, others the declaration God made by Moses. John Wesley keeps the received first person and explains it of the progenitors, since all the generations of Israel make one body and are sometimes spoken of as one person; the language he takes for Egyptian, unfamiliar because they lived apart. Ellicott is exercised by a different word, arguing that the verb of going out cannot have Israel for subject on any sense of the preposition, so God must be the subject, moving over or against the land of Egypt. Delitzsch fills in the burdens, the basket for carrying clay and bricks, and cites a papyrus naming the people who dragged stones for the great watchtower of the city of Rameses.
6:
God's own speech begins with the burdens of Egypt. John Gill has the heavy loads of bricks carried on the shoulder; Charles Ellicott, working from the root of the second noun, refers it to boiling and so to the potteries which with the brick-kilns made up the scene of the forced labour, and sets aside the Greek and Latin reading that puts a basket here, since the basket on the Egyptian monuments is what the previous clause means. Keil and Delitzsch describe the turn the discourse takes here, from festival to sorrow and awe, Israel's disobedience having frustrated the gracious purpose of its God's commandments and promises; the two names, my people and Israel, alternate as in the prophet's complaint.

Where the answering happened, and what it was, divides the voices. Adam Clarke places it at Sinai, where God was heard but not seen. John Wesley places it at the sea, the thunder coming from the dark and cloudy pillar against the Egyptians. Ellicott declines the received verb altogether, holding that a scholar is right to derive it from a root meaning to cover rather than to answer, so the line says God sheltered his people in the thundercloud, with plain allusion to the pillar of cloud and the same verb used elsewhere of spreading a cloud for a covering. He also reads the recital as liturgical, the rehearsal of God's past dealings customary at the autumn feast, delivered as though the feast were in progress.

The call to hear is treated as an astonishment. Matthew Henry turns it into a question — who should hear God if his own people will not, since he has already heard and answered them — and observes that the demand is not merely for a hearing but for being ruled; and yet, reasonable as it is, God puts an if upon it, because their neck is an iron sinew. C.H. Spurgeon asks whether the people can be so insensible as to be deaf to God himself, notes that he has to ask earnestly for a hearing, and turns it on the reader: we are not fond of being upbraided, and fly even from gentle reproofs — the deaf adder being no more grovelling than a man who will not hearken.

The prohibition of a strange god is read inwardly by both who take it up. Gill defines the strange god by what engrosses a man rather than what stands in a shrine: whatever a man loves most or trusts in is his god, so friend or relation, wife or children may be set up in God's place; the epicure makes a god of his belly, the covetous man of his money, the self-righteous man of his own righteousness. Spurgeon takes the second clause as the consequence of the first, since where false gods are their worship follows, and adds that a man is so desperate an idolater that the image is always a temptation — while the nests remain, the birds will be eager to return.

The promise that closes the passage is given two very different illustrations. Clarke keeps it abstract: let a man's desires be as extensive as they will, God undertakes to gratify them on condition of faithfulness, so that he shall lack no manner of thing that is good. Ellicott supplies a picture from custom, reporting that a Persian king wishing to honour a visitor would tell him to open his mouth wide and then cram it with sweetmeats and sometimes jewels, and that it remains a mark of politeness in the East to tear off the daintiest pieces of meat for a guest and either set them before him or put them in his mouth. Henry keeps to the ground of the promise rather than its figure, reminding the people what they owe to one who speaks as the Lord their God and redeemer from Egypt.
11:
The refusal is stated first, and John Gill gives it a figure from elsewhere in the Psalter: they were like the deaf adder that stops its ear against the charmer's voice, and would hearken neither to the law nor to the Gospel. What follows is the gravest sentence in the psalm. Gill ranks it above ordinary chastisement: God sometimes gave them into the hands of Moabites or Philistines, but to be delivered up to one's own heart's lust is worse than that, and worse even than being delivered to Satan, since salvation may follow the one and damnation the other. He adds that it is nonetheless righteous, since men who do not care to retain God in their knowledge are justly given over to a mind that cannot judge; and that nothing is more eagerly wanted than one's own heart's lust, and no judgment heavier than being granted it. Adam Clarke describes the mechanism: God withdrew the restraining grace they had abused, leaving them to their own inventions. Charles Ellicott corrects the noun, taking it not for lust but for stubbornness or perversity, from a root meaning to twist.

The wish that follows is read two ways. Gill treats it as a theological problem: the words express not God's purposing will, since no one has resisted that and he could have given them ears to hear, but his commanding and approving will, that men should hearken to the declarations he has made. Clarke does not raise the question, and praises the Hebrew instead: nothing can be more plaintive than the original, in which sense and sound are surprisingly united, and he will say to any reader of Hebrew, however learned, that he has never found in any poet, Greek or Latin, a finer example of deep-seated grief unable to express itself without interruptions of sighs and sobs, ending in a mournful cry. Keil and Delitzsch print these closing verses without any comment, the block breaking off at the quotation.

What the obedience would have purchased comes in three stages. On the subduing of enemies Gill notes that the verb means to bring them to their knees; Clarke draws the consequence for the promise, that where it appeared to fail it was because they rejected his counsel, and that while they were faithful they prospered, not one jot of God's word failing them. On the submission of God's haters Gill prefers a harder rendering, that they should have lied unto him — a feigned submission rather than a change of mind — and instances the emperor said to have cried when wounded that the Galilean had overcome him. Ellicott takes the pronoun differently, referring the submission to Israel rather than God, since the Lord's enemies are Israel's too, and explains the shift of number in the next clause as one of the sudden changes frequent in Hebrew poetry: Israel as a nation would have continued to prosper. Clarke puts the same clause plainly, that their prosperity would have known no end.

The last verse is difficult in grammar and rich in history. Ellicott sets out the problem: rendered properly it says he fed them with the finest of the wheat and satisfied thee with honey out of the rock, but the change of person is harsh and the past tense sits badly where nothing in fact happened, so he would slightly alter the pointing to give would feed. Gill and John Wesley keep the received sense, Gill noting that the Hebrew has the fat of the wheat, Wesley taking the honey for all pleasant and precious fruits. Clarke closes by quoting an old English psalter's version in its own spelling, with its paraphrase reading the wheat of the body of Christ and spiritual understanding, and the honey running from the stone of a wisdom sweet to the heart; several of the fathers, he notes, understood the place of Christ.
